In the years to come they will say, “They fell like the leaves In the autumn of nineteen thirty-nine.” November has come to the forest, To the meadows where we picked the cyclamen. The year fades with the white frost On the brown sedge in the hazy meadows, Where the deer tracks were black in the morning. Ice forms in the shadows; Disheveled maples hang over the water; Deep gold sunlight glistens on the shrunken stream. Somnolent trout move through pillars of brown and gold. The yellow maple leaves eddy above them, The glittering leaves of the cottonwood, The olive, velvety alder leaves, The scarlet dogwood leaves, Most poignant of all. In the afternoon thin blades of cloud Move over the mountains; The storm clouds follow them; Fine rain falls without wind. The forest is filled with wet resonant silence. When the rain pauses the clouds Cling to the cliffs and the waterfalls. In the evening the wind changes; Snow falls in the sunset. We stand in the snowy twilight And watch the moon rise in a breach of cloud. Between the black pines lie narrow bands of moonlight, Glimmering with floating snow. An owl cries in the sifting darkness. The moon has a sheen like a glacier.

outputs.L1:
In the years to come, they will say,  
“They fell like the leaves  
in the autumn of nineteen thirty-nine.”

November has come to the forest,  
to the meadows where we picked the cyclamen.  
The year fades with the white frost  
on the brown sedge in the hazy meadows,  
where the deer tracks were black in the morning.

Ice forms in the shadows;  
disheveled maples hang over the water;  
deep-gold sunlight glistens on the shrunken stream.  
Somnolent trout move through pillars of brown and gold.  
Above them eddy the yellow maple leaves,  
the glittering leaves of the cottonwood,  
the olive, velvety alder leaves,  
and the scarlet dogwood leaves—  
most poignant of all.

In the afternoon, thin blades of cloud  
move over the mountains;  
the storm clouds follow them;  
fine rain falls without wind.  
The forest is filled with a wet, resonant silence.

When the rain pauses, the clouds  
cling to the cliffs and the waterfalls.  
In the evening, the wind changes;  
snow falls in the sunset.

We stand in the snowy twilight  
and watch the moon rise through a breach in the clouds.  
Between the black pines lie narrow bands of moonlight,  
glimmering with floating snow.  
An owl cries in the sifting darkness.  
The moon has the sheen of a glacier.
outputs.L2:
Future generations will remember them by saying,  
“In the autumn of 1939, they dropped as leaves do.”

November now settles over the woods  
and across the fields where we once gathered cyclamen.  
The dying year whitens the brown sedge with frost  
throughout the mist-veiled meadows,  
where, at daybreak, deer prints appeared dark against the ground.

Ice gathers wherever shade lingers.  
Untidy maples lean above the water,  
while rich, golden sunlight flashes on the diminished stream.  
Drowsy trout drift among columns of gold and brown.  
Overhead, leaves spiral in the current:  
yellow maple,  
shining cottonwood,  
soft olive alder,  
and—more affecting than all the others—  
the crimson foliage of dogwood.

By afternoon, slender streaks of cloud  
cross the mountains,  
with heavy storm clouds advancing behind them.  
A delicate rain descends through motionless air,  
and the forest resonates with a damp, profound stillness.  
Whenever the rain relents, clouds remain wrapped  
around the cliffs and waterfalls.

At dusk, the wind turns.  
Snow begins to fall against the sunset.  
We remain in the white twilight,  
watching the moon emerge through an opening in the clouds.  
Thin ribbons of moonlight stretch between the dark pines,  
shimmering as snowflakes float through them.  
An owl calls from the filtering darkness.  
The moon gleams with the polished luster of glacial ice.
outputs.L3:
Future generations will remember those who died in 1939 as countless lives swept away like autumn leaves—each one distinct, yet all carried off by the same merciless wind of history.

In November, the countryside undergoes a quiet and solemn transformation. Frost whitens the forest floor, and thin sheets of ice form along the edges of pools and streams. The meadows lose their summer brightness as grasses wither and flowers fade, while the streams shrink and move more slowly through the cold earth. Above the trout gliding beneath the surface, red, yellow, and bronze leaves drift across brown-and-gold water.

Rain darkens the trees, and heavy clouds press low over the landscape. Waterfalls echo among the rocks, their steady roar rising from an otherwise profound and resonant silence. The forest seems to listen, holding within it a grief too deep for words.

By evening, snow begins to fall. Moonlight settles over the frozen ground, giving the woods a pale and spectral beauty. From somewhere among the shadowed branches comes the lonely cry of an owl. Its voice deepens the stillness, leaving the landscape cold, mournful, and unforgettable.
outputs.L4:
The poem evokes the approaching mass deaths of 1939 by tracing November’s gradual movement from autumn into winter. Its sequence of natural images—falling leaves, persistent rain, gathering snow, restless wildlife, and diminishing light—creates a landscape in which beauty is inseparable from disappearance. At first, the seasonal changes may seem familiar and even picturesque, but each detail contributes to a growing sense of unease. Leaves do not merely fall; they suggest lives being cut off. Rain darkens the world, snow covers what remains, and the shortening days make the future appear increasingly uncertain.

Nature’s decline also gives the poem a wider historical resonance. Written in the shadow of war, its November landscape becomes more than a description of the season: it anticipates the destruction and mass bereavement that would define 1939 and the years that followed. The retreat of animals and the fading of warmth imply instinctive withdrawal before danger, while the weakening light suggests the loss of security, hope, and human order. Because the poem approaches catastrophe indirectly, through changes in weather and landscape, its foreboding is especially powerful. History seems to enter the natural world before it is openly named.

The poem therefore transforms autumn beauty into an elegy for lives not yet lost. Its images remain visually vivid, but their beauty is fragile, shadowed by the knowledge that everything living is moving toward silence and death. November becomes both a literal month and a symbolic threshold between life and extinction, peace and war. By making seasonal decline mirror human mortality, the poem presents the coming conflict as a vast winter descending upon Europe. The result is a restrained but haunting meditation on impermanence, in which the ordinary death of the year foreshadows the extraordinary human losses soon to come.
outputs.L5:
They arrived in November, when the trees had surrendered their final leaves and the sky had turned the color of ash. No one knew where they came from or why they waited at the edge of the village each evening.

The wind carried their whispers through empty streets, but the words remained unclear. Behind locked doors, people listened and wondered.

Then, on the last night of November, the strangers disappeared.

The only thing they left behind was a message carved into the frozen earth:

**“The winter is only the beginning.”**

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem about November 1939, contrasting the beauty of an autumn forest with the foreboding of war.
counterfactuals.output:
**November, 1939**

The forest has spent its gold  
without regret.

Beech leaves lie bright as old coins  
beneath the rain,  
and the birches lift their pale arms  
into a sky rinsed clean and cold.

Along the path, mushrooms gather  
in the hush of roots.  
A fox crosses once—  
a brief flame  
between the black pines.

Everything seems prepared for sleep:

the stream under its glassy breath,  
the nests emptied of song,  
the last red berries  
holding fast against frost.

But beyond the hills  
trains move through the dark,  
their iron voices low and unending.

Maps open on tables.  
Borders bleed beneath pencils.  
Names of towns are spoken  
as if already lost.

The wind carries no gunfire yet,  
only the scent of wet bark,  
woodsmoke,  
apples stored in cellars—

and still the crows rise suddenly,  
all at once,  
like scraps of a burned letter.

November closes its beautiful hand.

Under the leaves, the earth waits.  
Above the earth, the branches tremble  
though the air is still.

Somewhere, boots are being issued.  
Somewhere, a mother sews a name  
inside a coat.

And the forest, innocent of history,  
lets fall  
one perfect copper leaf  
after another.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an elegiac nature poem that begins, “In the years to come they will say,” and includes falling leaves, cyclamen, trout, rain, snow, moonlight, and an owl.
counterfactuals.output:
In the years to come they will say,  
the hills remembered us awhile—  
our footsteps under falling leaves,  
our names unfastened from the stile.

Cyclamen burned beside the stones,  
small crimson lamps the dusk blew through;  
beneath the bridge, the trout lay still  
in water dark as tempered blue.

Then rain erased the summer paths,  
and snow made silence of the plain;  
moonlight entered the empty house  
and touched each window like a name.

Only an owl, among the pines,  
called once across the whitening air—  
as if to ask what we had loved,  
and why we were no longer there.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a vivid modernist poem set in late autumn, moving chronologically from a frosty morning through an afternoon storm to a snowy moonlit evening.
counterfactuals.output:
**November Triptych**

At dawn, the fields are glass—  
each thistle wired with frost,  
each fence-post shouldering  
a small white silence.

The sun rises like a struck match  
behind the warehouses.  
Crows lift, black punctuation  
from the stubbled sentence of earth.

By noon, roofs sweat silver.  
The road loosens into mud;  
bare trees click their branches  
over the passing cars.

Then the west goes iron.

Rain arrives sideways—  
drums the windows,  
flings dead leaves against brick  
like telegrams from a ruined country.

Thunder rearranges the rooms.  
Gutters choke. The river  
climbs its dark ladder  
under the bridge.

Toward evening, the storm breaks open.  
Rain whitens in the streetlights,  
hesitates—  
becomes snow.

Now chimneys fade.  
Footsteps fill behind themselves.  
The town withdraws  
into blue-lit squares.

Above it, the moon:  
a cold coin, a blind clock,  
sailing the torn clouds.

Snow gathers on the last red apple,  
on the bicycle’s empty frame,  
on the black mouth of the station—

and all night  
autumn disappears  
without a sound.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a melancholic pastoral poem in the style of Kenneth Rexroth, using precise images of maples, cottonwoods, alders, dogwoods, mountain clouds, and waterfalls.
counterfactuals.output:
I can’t write exactly in Kenneth Rexroth’s style, but I can offer an original poem with spare, contemplative imagery and a melancholic pastoral mood.

**After the Long Rains**

Maples darken beside the road,  
their wet leaves holding  
the last red light.

Across the river, cottonwoods  
lift pale undersides to the wind—  
a thousand small farewells.

Alders lean over the gravel bar.  
Among their roots, clear water  
threads the abandoned nests of trout.

The dogwoods have lost their flowers.  
Only the crooked branches remain,  
white with mountain mist.

Clouds travel the high passes  
without grief or destination.  
All afternoon the waterfalls  
unravel from the snowfields,

their voices arriving long after  
the water has fallen.

I stand where we once stood,  
beneath the dripping maple,  
and listen until evening

fills the valley like smoke—  
until each tree is only darkness,  
and the river carries darkness away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a lyrical meditation in which the autumn of 1939 becomes a metaphor for death and historical catastrophe, while the speaker observes a forest changing from rain to snow.
counterfactuals.output:
In the autumn of 1939, the rain fell with the patience of mourning. It darkened the trunks of the forest and gathered in the hollows of leaves, where the last gold trembled like a candle cupped against the wind. Beyond the trees, borders were breaking. Cities learned the weight of engines overhead; names vanished from maps before they vanished from memory.

I walked beneath the branches and listened. Each drop seemed to strike an invisible bell. The beeches let go their copper, the birches their pale coins, as if the whole wood were paying passage to the dead. Yet no ferryman appeared—only the river, swollen and brown, carrying twigs, feathers, and rumors toward an unseen sea.

Then the rain began to whiten.

At first, snow mingled with it shyly, a few cold syllables dissolving on the earth. Soon the air filled with ash that was not ash, with feathers no bird had shed. The forest withdrew into itself. Paths blurred. Roots disappeared. Every stump received a little shroud.

How gently catastrophe resembles peace from a distance. The fields lay quiet under their whitening sky; roofs softened; the guns beyond the horizon became a dull weather of their own. Snow covered the leaves, the leaves covered the mud, and the mud covered what no season could forgive.

By nightfall, the world had lost its colors. I stood among the trees while winter entered them—slow, absolute, without anger. Death was not a door but this gradual erasure: rain turning to snow, voices turning to numbers, countries turning to silence.

Still, beneath the snow, the fallen leaves kept their ruined gold.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
